questions.text: A pilot's last FAA medical certificate was issued in 2004 and was never renewed. They hold a valid U.S. driver's license and complete a CMEC physical and online course today. Can they legally operate under BasicMed?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — any prior FAA medical certificate qualifies regardless of issue date, because Part 68 only verifies that a certificate was issued at some point in the pilot's history

options.label: B
options.text: No — BasicMed requires the pilot to have held a valid FAA medical certificate issued after July 14, 2006, and a 2004 certificate does not satisfy this requirement

options.label: C
options.text: No — BasicMed is only available to pilots whose most recent medical was denied or revoked, as it was designed as a pathway for those who failed the AME process

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the CMEC physical and online course are all that is required to qualify for BasicMed, and prior medical history has no bearing on eligibility

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 68.3 and 61.113(i) require that the pilot must have held a valid FAA medical certificate issued after July 14, 2006 — the date Public Law 114-190 took effect. This requirement ensures the FAA has a baseline medical record on file. A 2004 certificate predates this statutory requirement. The certificate must also not have been suspended, revoked, or withdrawn; a simple expiration is acceptable. Option D is incorrect — BasicMed was designed as a simpler alternative for all eligible GA pilots, not as a reinstatement pathway.

questions.text: A CFI operating under BasicMed is offered $150 per hour to provide primary flight instruction in a student's Piper Archer — a normal-category ASEL aircraft with a max certificated takeoff weight of 2,550 lbs. Which statement about this flight is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: This flight is legal — CFIs may receive compensation for flight instruction under BasicMed because payment is for the act of teaching, not for acting as pilot in command of the aircraft

options.label: B
options.text: This flight is legal but only if both the CFI and student share the cost equally, since BasicMed allows pro rata expense sharing under the same rules as 14 CFR 61.113(c)

options.label: C
options.text: This flight is prohibited — BasicMed only authorizes solo operations; any flight with a second person aboard converts the CFI to a for-hire PIC regardless of who is paying

options.label: D
options.text: This flight is prohibited — BasicMed regulations contain an absolute ban on all compensation or hire with no exceptions for flight instruction or crew duties

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 61.113(i) prohibits BasicMed operations 'for compensation or hire' meaning the pilot cannot be paid to fly the aircraft as a transport service. However, the FAA has consistently interpreted CFI compensation as payment for instruction, not for holding the controls. The CFI is a required crewmember in instructional context, but their compensation is tied to the educational service rendered. This same logic allows CFIs to log instruction time while a student is the sole manipulator. Options A and B misstate the regulation; Option C introduces a pro rata framework that does not apply to instructional compensation.

questions.text: A pilot operating under BasicMed wants to fly a Piper Navajo Chieftain with a max certificated takeoff weight of 7,000 lbs. They plan to remove 3 of the 8 seats, reducing occupancy to 5 people including the pilot. Is this flight legal under BasicMed?

options.label: A
options.text: No — BasicMed prohibits all multi-engine aircraft operations regardless of weight, occupant configuration, or installed equipment on the specific flight

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — removing seats reduces the certified occupant capacity below 6, and with light fuel loading the actual takeoff weight falls below 6,000 lbs, satisfying both BasicMed limits

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — the 6,000-lb limit applies to the weight at the moment of takeoff, and a lightly fueled Navajo can easily depart below that threshold on short trips

options.label: D
options.text: No — BasicMed's 6,000-lb limitation applies to the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight per its type certificate, which cannot be changed by removing seats or reducing payload

questions.explanation: The BasicMed weight limitation under 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) explicitly refers to 'maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds' — this is the aircraft's type-certificated limit, not the actual weight at takeoff. The Navajo's type certificate specifies 7,000 lbs; that number cannot be changed by removing seats or reducing fuel. Options C and D conflate the certificated limit with the actual operating weight. Option B incorrectly prohibits all multi-engine operations — BasicMed has no such restriction if the aircraft meets the weight and occupant limits.

questions.text: A 500-hour Cessna 172 pilot rents a Piper Cherokee for the first time. During preflight, they notice the fuel selector has LEFT / RIGHT / OFF positions — no BOTH setting like their Cessna. They plan a 2-hour cross-country. What is the PRIMARY accident risk for this flight?

options.label: A
options.text: Negative transfer from Cessna fuel management habits may cause the pilot to mismanage the Cherokee's tank selector, a leading cause of power loss in unfamiliar aircraft

options.label: B
options.text: The primary risk is spatial disorientation caused by the Cherokee's lower seating position and restricted over-the-nose visibility compared to a high-wing Cessna configuration

options.label: C
options.text: The Cherokee's low-wing design places the fuel tanks below the engine, reversing the gravity-feed direction and dramatically increasing the likelihood of vapor lock at cruise altitude

options.label: D
options.text: The 500-hour pilot lacks the minimum experience threshold FAA regulations require before transitioning between high-wing and low-wing aircraft of the same category and class

questions.explanation: Fuel mismanagement is the leading cause of engine failure accidents in unfamiliar aircraft (FAA ASIAS data). Negative transfer occurs when a habit from one aircraft causes an error in another. A Cessna pilot is conditioned to a 'BOTH' fuel position — left on, right on, both on, always. The Cherokee requires deliberate tank switching every 30 minutes. If the pilot forgets to switch (or does not understand the system), one tank runs dry while the other is full, causing an unnecessary engine failure. AC 90-109A specifically identifies fuel system differences as a high-priority transition training item. Options A and B contain factual errors; Option D is a minor distraction risk, not the primary accident cause.

questions.text: A pilot completed their BasicMed CMEC physical on March 5, 2022, and their online medical education course on April 10, 2022. It is now April 11, 2024. Which of their BasicMed credentials, if any, has expired?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither credential has expired — the CMEC physical is valid for 48 months and the online course is valid for 36 calendar months, so both remain current through 2025

options.label: B
options.text: The online course has expired — it is valid for 24 calendar months from April 2022 through April 30, 2024, while the CMEC physical remains valid for 48 months until March 5, 2026

options.label: C
options.text: Both credentials have expired — the CMEC physical has a 24-month validity identical to the online course, so both expired sometime in early 2024

options.label: D
options.text: The CMEC physical has expired — it is valid for 24 months like the online course, meaning it expired on March 5, 2024, while the online course remains valid through April 2026

questions.explanation: Under 14 CFR Part 68, the two BasicMed credentials have different validity periods. The CMEC physical examination is valid for 48 months to the day from the date of the examination — March 5, 2022 to March 5, 2026. The online medical education course is valid for 24 calendar months — April 2022 through the end of April 2024. Since it is now April 11, 2024, the course has not yet expired (it expires April 30, 2024) but is very close. Note the critical distinction: CMEC uses exact days (48 months to the day), while the course uses calendar months (extended to end of the month). Option A incorrectly assigns a 24-month validity to the CMEC. Options C and D contain incorrect validity durations.

questions.text: A steam-gauge pilot transitioning to a Cirrus SR22 is told by the seller that the Garmin Perspective+ autopilot is in VS (Vertical Speed) mode, climbing at 500 fpm toward 8,500 feet. The pilot assumes the autopilot will automatically level off at the target altitude. What will actually happen?

options.label: A
options.text: The autopilot will begin a programmed 50-fpm deceleration at 300 feet below the target altitude, reaching zero climb rate precisely at 8,500 feet regardless of the VS setting

options.label: B
options.text: The autopilot will capture and hold 8,500 feet automatically when within 200 feet of the target, since all Garmin autopilots feature mandatory altitude capture in VS mode to prevent overshoot

options.label: C
options.text: The autopilot will continue climbing past 8,500 feet indefinitely at 500 fpm — VS mode maintains a constant vertical speed and does not capture a target altitude without pilot intervention

options.label: D
options.text: The autopilot will level off only if the altitude pre-selector was set before engaging VS mode; if it was set afterward, the capture function is disabled until the mode is cycled

questions.explanation: This is a textbook automation surprise scenario documented in AC 90-109A. VS (Vertical Speed) mode commands a fixed rate of climb or descent — it does not capture an altitude. To automatically level off, the pilot must engage ALT (Altitude Hold) mode or use FLC (Flight Level Change) mode with a preselected altitude, which does capture on the Garmin system. A pilot transitioning from steam gauges who assumes 'autopilot on = it will level off' will overshoot the target altitude, potentially entering IMC or busting an ATC clearance altitude. Options A, B, and C describe behaviors that do not exist in VS mode on the Garmin Perspective+ system.

questions.text: You are a 400-hour Cessna 172 pilot. A friend offers you a free week with their Beechcraft Bonanza F33A. You are rated ASEL and the Bonanza does not require a type rating. You have never flown a retractable-gear, low-wing aircraft. All options are legal. Which is SAFEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Accept, study the POH on the ground for 2 hours, then depart on the first day with a friend aboard to get real-world feedback during the initial transition flights

options.label: B
options.text: Decline the offer entirely — transitioning to a retractable-gear aircraft without a formal type endorsement creates unacceptable legal and insurance liability for all planned flights

options.label: C
options.text: Accept and fly the Bonanza immediately — 400 hours of ASEL experience means you are rated and proficient, and the transition risk from a 172 to an F33A is widely overstated for experienced pilots

options.label: D
options.text: Accept, then schedule 2 to 3 hours of dual instruction with a Bonanza-qualified CFI before flying solo, treating the first flights as proficiency-building sessions without passengers

questions.sjt_rationale: All four options are legal — no type rating or endorsement is required for the Bonanza F33A (non-complex, non-high-performance). Option A dismisses the risk based on total hours, ignoring that transition accidents happen precisely because pilots assume hours in one type transfer to another (macho). Option B accepts known risk — first flight in an unfamiliar aircraft with a passenger aboard compounds any error (get-there-itis disguised as preparation). Option C treats a manageable situation as hopeless — structured training exists precisely for this scenario (resignation). Option D follows AC 90-109A guidance: get dual instruction in type, treat early flights as test flights, introduce passengers only after demonstrating proficiency.
questions.explanation: AC 90-109A documents the Bonanza transition as a specific high-risk scenario due to the retractable gear and low-wing fuel management differences from the Cessna 172. The 'gear-up landing' accident is disproportionately common in pilots new to retractables — not because the aircraft is difficult, but because the habit of not checking gear position does not exist in fixed-gear pilots. Dual instruction builds the new habit before it matters.

questions.text: You are flying your first solo cross-country in a glass-cockpit aircraft. In cruise flight, the autopilot unexpectedly enters an unfamiliar mode and the aircraft begins a 300-fpm descent you did not command. You are in VMC with 5,000 feet AGL. All options are legal. Which is SAFEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue on course while referencing the quick-start guide in the seat pocket — diagnosing the autopilot in flight is the most efficient way to restore normal operations without delay

options.label: B
options.text: Continue analyzing the autopilot mode display for up to 2 minutes before taking control — correctly identifying the mode allows you to fix the root cause rather than masking it by disconnecting

options.label: C
options.text: Disconnect the autopilot immediately, hand-fly the aircraft to maintain altitude, then assess the situation from a stable configuration before deciding whether to continue or divert

options.label: D
options.text: Immediately turn back to the departure airport and declare a precautionary emergency — any autopilot anomaly on a first solo cross-country constitutes an in-flight emergency requiring ATC assistance

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A allows a 300-fpm uncontrolled descent to continue while the pilot studies a display — prioritizing diagnosis over aircraft control (macho, inverted priorities). At 5,000 AGL and 300 fpm, the pilot has roughly 16 minutes before terrain contact in flat terrain; less if the descent rate increases. Option B over-reacts — an autopilot mode confusion in VMC is not an emergency if the pilot hand-flies the aircraft (resignation). Option C uses a reference guide while the aircraft is descending unmonitored (get-there-itis). Option D follows the foundational aviation rule: aviate first. Disconnect the automation, stabilize the aircraft, then assess. This is the explicit guidance in AC 90-109A for automation surprise scenarios.
questions.explanation: Automation surprise is defined as a situation where the pilot does not know what the automation is doing or why. The correct response is always: remove the automation, regain manual control, stabilize the aircraft, then assess. FAA-H-8083-25C Chapter 2 and AC 90-109A both state that hand-flying proficiency must always be maintained as the baseline skill — automation is a tool, not a substitute for stick-and-rudder ability. NTSB studies of TAA accidents show that pilots who attempted to troubleshoot autopilot anomalies while the aircraft was in an abnormal state consistently produced worse outcomes than pilots who immediately disconnected and hand-flew.
